steps.tx: A pediatric **supracondylar fracture** of the humerus is the most common elbow break in children between five and eight years old. Over ninety-five percent are extension-type injuries caused by a fall onto an outstretched hand with hyperextended elbow. Thinning of the supracondylar cortex by the olecranon and coronoid fossae creates an inherent structural stress riser vulnerable to hyperextension loading.
steps.say: Supracondylar humeral fractures are the most common elbow fractures in young children, peaking around five to eight years. Over ninety-five percent are extension injuries caused by a fall on an outstretched hand. The thin bone between the olecranon and coronoid fossae easily buckles under hyperextension stress.

steps.tx: The widely used **Gartland classification** stratifies extension fractures based on cortical contact and displacement on plain radiographs. Type I is non-displaced. Type II is displaced with an intact posterior cortical hinge. Type III demonstrates complete displacement with total loss of cortical continuity. Type IV exhibits multidirectional instability during flexion and extension due to complete circumferential periosteal rupture.
steps.say: Gartland classifies extension fractures into four grades. Type one is completely nondisplaced. Type two is displaced but retains an intact posterior cortical hinge. Type three is completely displaced with no cortical contact. Type four has complete circumferential soft tissue stripping, making it unstable in both flexion and extension.

vis.title: Gartland Classification Summary
rows: Posterior slab at 90 degrees for 3 weeks
Urgent closed reduction and K-wire fixation
Operative pinning; open reduction if unstable

steps.tx: Radiographic assessment relies on the **anterior humeral line** and Baumann angle. On a true lateral elbow radiograph, a line drawn down the anterior cortex of the humerus must intersect the middle third of the ossified capitellum. In extension-type fractures, this line passes entirely anterior to the capitellum, proving posterior displacement even when subtle on frontal views.
steps.say: Always check the anterior humeral line on the lateral X-ray. A straight line down the anterior humerus must slice through the middle third of the capitellar ossification center. If the capitellum lies posterior to this line, an extension fracture is confirmed. Also check Baumann angle to ensure there is no varus tilt.

left.title: Anterior Humeral Line
points: Must bisect middle third of capitellum

right.title: Baumann Angle Metrics
points: Angle between humeral axis and physis

steps.tx: The devastating vascular complication of **Volkmann ischaemia** develops when sharp proximal bone fragments compress or lacerate the brachial artery in the tight antecubital space. Persistent forearm compartment swelling leads to irreversible flexor muscle infarction and clawing contracture. Severe unremitting forearm pain aggravated by passive extension of the fingers is the earliest and most reliable warning sign.
steps.say: Watch like a hawk for Volkmann ischemia. The proximal bone spike can kinking or lacerate the brachial artery, causing compartmental necrosis of forearm flexor muscles. Severe pain on passive extension of the fingers is the earliest warning. Never wait for pulselessness to act.

steps.tx: Definitive management of unstable fractures demands **percutaneous pinning** with Kirschner wires under fluoroscopic guidance following gentle closed reduction. Two or three divergent lateral entry pins provide rigid bi-cortical stability without risking the ulnar nerve. If a medial pin is deemed necessary for torsional rigidity, it must be inserted with the elbow extended to prevent ulnar nerve entrapment.
steps.say: Stabilize Gartland type two and three fractures with closed reduction and percutaneous K-wires. Two or three divergent lateral pins give excellent stability while avoiding the ulnar nerve entirely. If a medial wire is placed, extend the elbow slightly and palpate the groove to avoid impaling the ulnar nerve.

left.title: Lateral Divergent Pins
points: Two or three lateral entry wires
Zero risk of ulnar nerve injury

right.title: Crossed Pin Configuration
points: Carries 2 to 4 percent ulnar palsy risk

quiz.q: Where should the anterior humeral line pass on a normal pediatric lateral elbow radiograph?
options: Through the middle third of the capitellar ossification center
Entirely anterior to the ossified capitellum
Posterior to the olecranon fossa line
Through the center of the radial head physis
quiz.explain: On a true lateral radiograph of a normal elbow, the anterior humeral line passes through the middle third of the capitellum. In extension fractures, the capitellum lies posterior to it.

quiz.q: What is the earliest and most reliable clinical sign of impending Volkmann ischaemia?
options: Disproportionate pain exacerbated by passive finger extension
Absence of a palpable radial pulse at the wrist
Complete motor paralysis of the anterior interosseous nerve
Severe subcutaneous pallor of the hand
quiz.explain: Severe pain elicited by passive finger extension is the earliest, most reliable bedside warning of rising flexor compartment pressure and impending Volkmann ischaemia.
